extracted.intended_audience: graduate students or advanced undergraduates studying algebraic geometry; readers of Ravi Vakil's 'The Rising Sea'
extracted.subtask_description: Defines the intersection product of n line bundles with a coherent sheaf (or an n-dimensional closed subscheme) on an n-dimensional projective variety, and records its basic properties (symmetry, multilinearity, numerical invariance, field-extension invariance), key formulas (Asymptotic Riemann–Roch, projection formula), and related exercises (Bézout/degree, Cartier divisor compatibility).

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition: intersection product (L1 · · · Ln · F)
rubrics_metrics.description: Suppose F is a coherent sheaf on X with proper support of dimension at most n, and L1, ..., Ln are invertible sheaves on X. Define (L1 · · · Ln · F) to be the signed sum over the 2^n subsets of {1,...,n} of (−1)^m χ(X, L∨_{i1} ⊗ ··· ⊗ L∨_{im} ⊗ F).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is called the intersection of L1,...,Ln with F. When F is the structure sheaf of a closed subscheme Y of dimension ≤ n, write (L1 · · · Ln · Y). If all Li are equal to L, one often writes (L^n · F) or (L^n · Y). The parentheses/notation must be handled carefully: L^n means tensor power, not intersection product by itself.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interpretation for closed subschemes and notation conventions
rubrics_metrics.description: When F = O_Y for a closed subscheme Y (dim ≤ n), the symbol (L1 · · · Ln · Y) denotes the intersection product of L1,...,Ln with Y; if Y = X, one may write (L1 · · · Ln) with X implicit.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be explicit about parentheses when needed; the convention allows thinking of intersecting effective Cartier divisors rather than line bundles when convenient.

rubrics_metrics.name: Vanishing with trivial line bundle (Exercise 20.1.A)
rubrics_metrics.description: If L1 ≅ O_X, then (L1 · L2 · · · · Ln · F) = 0.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is a simple 'reality check' property of the intersection product, showing that a trivial factor yields zero.

rubrics_metrics.name: Curve-degree compatibility and Bézout (Exercise 20.1.B)
rubrics_metrics.description: (a) If X is a projective curve and L an invertible sheaf, then (L) = deg_X L. (b) Suppose k is infinite, X = P^N, and Y is an n-dimensional subvariety. If H1,...,Hn are general hypersurfaces of degrees d1,...,dn respectively, then deg(H1 ∩ ··· ∩ Hn ∩ Y) = d1 ··· dn · deg(Y), and correspondingly (O(H1) · ··· · O(Hn) · Y) = d1 ··· dn · deg(Y).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Part (b) is a version of Bézout’s theorem in this intersection-product language; it requires general choice (genericity) of hypersurfaces and an infinite base field hypothesis for the genericity argument.

rubrics_metrics.name: Compatibility with effective Cartier divisors (Exercise 20.1.C)
rubrics_metrics.description: If D is an effective Cartier divisor on X that restricts to an effective Cartier divisor D|_Y on Y (i.e., remains locally a nonzerodivisor on Y), then (L1 · · · Ln−1 · O(D) · Y) = (L1 · · · Ln−1 · D|_Y). More generally, if D does not contain any associated point of F, then (L1 · · · Ln−1 · O(D) · F) = (L1 · · · Ln−1 · F|_D).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This permits thinking of intersections with Cartier divisors as intersections with their restrictions; useful when moving between divisor and line-bundle language.

rubrics_metrics.name: Field-extension invariance (Exercise 20.1.D)
rubrics_metrics.description: The intersection product (L1 · · · Ln · F) is preserved under field extension of the base field k.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: One may therefore reduce to working over infinite/algebraically closed fields when proving general properties, using base change.

rubrics_metrics.name: Symmetry and multilinearity (Proposition 20.1.3)
rubrics_metrics.description: For X projective and fixed F, the function (L1,...,Ln) ↦ (L1 · · · Ln · F) is symmetric and multilinear in the Li.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof uses induction on n, reduction to the case of very ample line bundles, and vanishing tricks (dévissage). Key proof ingredients: write any line bundle as difference of two very ample bundles and use base-change/infinite-field reduction; Exercise hints guide the rewriting steps and vanishing checks.

rubrics_metrics.name: Vanishing for too many factors (Exercise 20.1.H)
rubrics_metrics.description: If dim Supp F < n+1, then the intersection product of n+1 invertible sheaves with F vanishes: (L1 · · · L_{n+1} · F) = 0.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This follows from the multilinear definition and is used in asymptotic/polynomiality arguments (e.g., to control degrees of Hilbert/Riemann–Roch polynomials).

rubrics_metrics.name: Numerical invariance (Proposition 20.1.4)
rubrics_metrics.description: For projective X, the intersection product depends only on the numerical equivalence classes of the Li (i.e., on degrees on curves).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The proof reduces to the case where one factor is very ample and then uses the Cartier divisor compatibility and inductive arguments; this implies intersection numbers are well-defined on N^1(X)_R.

rubrics_metrics.name: Asymptotic Riemann–Roch / leading coefficient identification (Exercise 20.1.I)
rubrics_metrics.description: If X is projective of dimension n and F a coherent sheaf with dim Supp F ≤ n, then χ(X, L^{⊗ m} ⊗ F) is a polynomial in m of degree ≤ n. The coefficient of m^n is (L^n · F)/n!.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the vanishing of the (n+1)-fold intersection and expand the intersection-definition recursion; this generalizes the curve Riemann–Roch leading-term interpretation to higher dimensions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Projection formula for degrees (Exercise 20.1.J)
rubrics_metrics.description: Suppose π : X1 → X2 is a projective morphism of integral projective varieties of the same dimension n, and L1,...,Ln are invertible sheaves on X2. Then (π^*L1 · · · π^*Ln) = deg(X1/X2) · (L1 · · · Ln).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is a compatibility of intersection numbers with finite surjective morphisms; use degree multiplicativity under composition and pullback of line bundles.

rubrics_metrics.name: Construction of the third-point morphism t on a cubic (elliptic) curve
rubrics_metrics.description: Given a plane cubic C and regular points p,q, define t(p,q) as the 'third' residual point of intersection of the line pq with C (for p=q, t(p,p) is the other intersection of the tangent). The third point is regular when p and q are regular. Locally, in affine coordinates with line x2 = m x1 + b, substitute into the cubic to get γ(x1) = A x1^3 + B x1^2 + C x1 + D; the third root is R1 = −B/A − P1 − Q1, and R2 = m R1 + b gives the third point as a rational function of P and Q on an open set (A ≠ 0).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This gives a local description of a morphism t on a Zariski-open subset; these local maps glue (uniquely) using that morphisms are determined by behavior on closed points (Exercise 11.4.B) and agree after base change (Exercise 10.2.J). The construction commutes with arbitrary base change; special handling is required over F2 (construct over F4 and then descend).

rubrics_metrics.name: Using t to define group variety structure on an elliptic curve
rubrics_metrics.description: On an elliptic curve E embedded via |O_E(3p)|, define identity e: Spec k → E sending Spec k to p, inversion i: E → E via q ↦ t(p,q) (composition described), and multiplication m: E × E → E by (q,r) ↦ t(p, t(q,r)). Then (E,e,i,m) is a group variety over k.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To verify the group axioms one checks equalities of the corresponding morphisms after base change to an algebraic closure (they agree on k-points because Pic^0(E) is a group), and then uses that morphisms of k-varieties are determined by their maps on k-points (Exercise 11.4.B) or that agreement after base change implies agreement (Exercise 10.2.J). All maps commute with base change.
